evidence_quotes.quote: In a randomized controlled trial, offering subsidies increased the likelihood of successful sales conversions
The sales closing rate among eligible households in treatment areas was 38% compared to 6% among ineligible treatment households.
Among subsidy-qualifying households, offering subsidies increased the village-level latrine purchase rate by 32% (p ¼ 0.00).
Offering targeted subsidies signiﬁcantly increases the likelihood of a household purchasing a latrine.
The latrine sales described here refer to orders, not installations.

findings.exact_estimate: Marginal probability = +0.313*** (p = 0.00; 99% confidence level; stated in text as 31 percentage points, p = 0.00); SEs clustered at village level across 30 villages (2,821 unique household sales presentations). Raw closing rate in treatment areas: 38% among subsidy-offered eligible households vs. 6% among ineligible households (p = 0.00).
findings.exposure_and_reference: Household in Treatment village & Eligible / Received 50% latrine price subsidy offer (Yes) vs. Base group: Control village & Not eligible / Received subsidy (No)
findings.finding_label: Primary household-level logistic regression: predicted probability of latrine purchase for subsidy-offered eligible households
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Household latrine purchase (binary indicator of ordering an Easy Latrine or Sky Latrine during sales presentation; higher values = BETTER household sanitation access/uptake)

findings.exact_estimate: Treatment & Not eligible (no subsidy): marginal probability = +0.0056 (p = 0.860) vs. Control & Not eligible (Base). Control & Eligible (no subsidy): marginal probability = +0.0132 (p = 0.416) vs. Control & Not eligible (Base). Descriptive purchase rates in control areas: 8% eligible vs. 6% ineligible (p = 0.32); in treatment areas: 6% ineligible. Only 3 of 2,352 non-purchasing households reported waiting on a subsidy.
findings.exposure_and_reference: (a) Treatment village & Not eligible (no subsidy) vs. Control village & Not eligible (Base); and (b) Control village & Eligible (no subsidy, retail price only) vs. Control village & Not eligible (Base)
findings.finding_label: Household-level logistic regression: non-eligible spillover / market distortion check and unsubsidized eligible comparison
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Household latrine purchase (binary indicator of ordering a latrine; higher values = BETTER household sanitation access/uptake)

findings.exact_estimate: Village-level OLS treatment effect = +23 percentage points higher village-level sales closing rate in treatment vs. control villages (p = 0.00, controlling for village-level climate vulnerability status; N = 30 villages; full table in Supporting Information Table 8). Across all household presentations, 22% led to a sale in treatment areas vs. 7% in control areas (p = 0.00), totaling 326 vs. 111 latrines ordered.
findings.exposure_and_reference: Village-level treatment assignment (50% targeted sanitation subsidies offered to eligible households, 15 villages) vs. Control villages (retail price only, no subsidies offered, 15 villages)
findings.finding_label: Primary village-level OLS regression: overall village latrine sales closing rate
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Village-level latrine sales closing / uptake rate across all approached households without a toilet (continuous proportion; higher values = BETTER community sanitation access/uptake)
findings.table_or_page: PDF Page 6 (referencing Supporting Information Table 8) and PDF Page 7

findings.exact_estimate: All subsidy-qualifying households: +32 percentage points increase in village-level latrine purchase rate (p = 0.00; printed as '32 percentage points' on p. 1 and '32% (p = 0.00)' on p. 6). PPI-qualifying (non-IDPoor) subgroup: +37 percentage points increase (p = 0.00). IDPoor-qualifying subgroup: +26 percentage points increase (printed as '26% increase', p = 0.03).
findings.exposure_and_reference: Village-level subsidy treatment offer vs. retail-price control among (a) all subsidy-qualifying households, (b) households qualifying via the Poverty Probability Index (PPI) with climate-adjusted thresholds, and (c) households qualifying via government IDPoor status
findings.finding_label: Village-level OLS regressions by target subgroup: all eligible, PPI-qualifying, and IDPoor-qualifying households
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Village-level latrine sales closing rate within each target subgroup (higher values = BETTER sanitation access/uptake among vulnerable households)

findings.exact_estimate: Household-level climate vulnerability moderation: among subsidy-offered households, the increase in purchase probability over baseline (ineligible control) was +10 percentage points larger for households reporting direct climate vulnerability in the past year (p = 0.00); among households not offered subsidies, direct household climate vulnerability had no statistically significant effect. Community-level CVI moderation: village-level interaction regressions showed the impact of offering subsidies was comparable regardless of community climate vulnerability (CVI) status (no significant difference).
findings.exposure_and_reference: Subsidy offer interacted with / stratified by (a) household-level direct climate shock in past year and (b) commune-level Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI) status
findings.finding_label: Climate-vulnerability heterogeneity at household and community levels
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Household predicted probability of latrine purchase and village-level latrine sales closing rate (higher values = BETTER sanitation access/uptake)

headline_result_summary: In a 30-village cluster-randomized controlled trial (2,821 unique household sales presentations) in rural Kampong Chhnang province, Cambodia, offering targeted 50% price subsidies (using government IDPoor status plus Poverty Probability Index thresholds adjusted for household and community climate vulnerability) substantially and significantly increased purchases of durable/climate-resilient latrines. Being offered a subsidy increased an eligible household's predicted probability of purchasing a latrine by 31.3 percentage points relative to ineligible control households (Table 1: +0.313, p = 0.00; raw closing rate 38% among subsidy-offered treatment households vs. 6% among ineligible treatment households and 8% among unsubsidized eligible control households). At the village level, offering targeted subsidies increased the overall latrine sales closing rate by 23 percentage points (p = 0.00; 22% vs. 7% across all sales presentations) and increased the village-level purchase rate among subsidy-qualifying households by 32 percentage points (p = 0.00), including +37 percentage points among PPI-qualifying households (p = 0.00) and +26 percentage points among IDPoor households (p = 0.03). Purchase rates among ineligible households did not differ between treatment and control villages (+0.0056, p = 0.860), indicating no market distortion.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Percentage vs. percentage-point wording: The authors intermittently write '%' when reporting linear/marginal probability differences in percentage points (e.g., Highlights: 'by 31%', p. 6: 'by 32% (p = 0.00)' and '26% increase', whereas the Abstract and Table 1 text state '32 percentage points', '31 percentage points (0.313)', and '37 percentage points'). Coders must not misread '31%' or '32%' as relative risk increases—they are percentage-point increases (e.g., ~8% to ~38–40%). 2. Reference category in Table 1: In Table 1 (p. 6), the base category for the +0.313 marginal probability is 'Control / Not eligible', not 'Control / Eligible' (+0.0132, p = 0.416); comparing 'Treatment / Eligible' directly to 'Control / Eligible' yields roughly a 30 percentage-point difference (38% vs. 8% raw rates; 32 pp at the village level). 3. Orders vs. installations: As noted in Limitations (pp. 8–9), the outcome variable captures latrine purchase orders during sales presentations rather than verified physical installations (typical iDE order cancellation rates are 10–20% and were not tracked during the 7.5-month pilot). 4. Differential targeting across arms: Subsidy eligibility was higher in treatment villages (51–52%) than control villages (45%, p = 0.00), driven by a 5 percentage-point higher share of IDPoor households identified in treatment villages (p = 0.00) because village authorities helped sales agents locate poor households without toilets more actively when subsidies were available. 5. Supporting Information tables: Full regression tables for the village-level OLS models (e.g., Table 8) and baseline balance checks reside in the online Supporting Information rather than the main 10-page PDF, and Table 1 does not specify in its caption whether the printed marginal probabilities come from the unadjusted base logit or the climate-controlled logit described on p. 5.
study_design: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (village-level random assignment stratified by commune climate vulnerability status) supplemented by 13 qualitative stakeholder interviews and programmatic cost-effectiveness analysis
unit_and_sample_size: 30 rural villages (15 treatment, 15 control; 23 designated climate-vulnerable [12 treatment, 11 control]) in Kampong Chhnang province, Tonle Sap Lake region; 2,821 unique household sales presentations to households without a toilet (after dropping 1,598 duplicate follow-up visits), yielding 437 latrine orders (326 treatment, 111 control) and 2,352 non-purchasing household responses; plus 13 qualitative interviews
